title: Trump Says on The View He Might Date Ivanka If She Were Not His Daughter
description_short: Trump Says on The View He Might Date Ivanka If She Were Not His Daughter
description_medium: On a 2006 episode of *The View*, Donald Trump said he might date his daughter Ivanka if she were not his daughter. The remark was made on the television show, not during the separate Howard Stern interview identified in the original entry. The two appearances included different comments and should not be conflated.
description_long: During a 2006 appearance on *The View*, Donald Trump said that if Ivanka were not his daughter, perhaps he would be dating her. The comment was part of a televised discussion about his daughter and her appearance. It was not made during the September 2006 Howard Stern interview, as the earlier version of this entry said. Trump made other sexualized comments about Ivanka in separate interviews, including with Stern, but those remarks belong to different occasions. Keeping the events separate matters because a documented quotation can still be misattributed to the wrong interview. The comment drew renewed attention as a public example of Trump speaking about his daughter in romantic terms. The entry concerns the *View* appearance and the specific dating remark; it does not combine it with the separate Stern interview or imply the statements were made at the same time. The corrected venue and date identify where the quotation belongs and preserve the distinction between the two media appearances.

title: Pandemic Response Team Disbanded
description_medium: The Trump administration had previously dismantled the National Security Council's global health security team in 2018, removing a critical line of defense against biological threats. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, the U.S. lacked the centralized leadership and preparedness this team was designed to provide. This administrative sabotage crippled the early response.
description_long: In 2018, the Trump administration reorganized the National Security Council and disbanded its global health security team. The team had coordinated planning for infectious-disease outbreaks and other biological threats. When COVID-19 emerged, the United States no longer had that dedicated NSC unit. The change became a focus of criticism over pandemic preparedness, but the record does not identify which responsibilities were transferred or show how the reorganization affected particular federal decisions during the early response. Those links are needed to establish how much the team’s removal contributed to the response’s failures.

title: Qatar Blockade Coincides With Scrutiny of Kushner Family's 666 Fifth Avenue Financing Efforts
description_short: Qatar Blockade Coincides With Scrutiny of Kushner Family's 666 Fifth Avenue Financing Efforts
description_medium: Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, and Egypt severed relations with and blockaded Qatar in June 2017, and President Trump publicly backed the move. Separately, the Kushner family had sought financing for its heavily indebted 666 Fifth Avenue property from potential foreign investors. The timing prompted conflict-of-interest scrutiny, but the evidence reviewed does not establish that a Qatari financing refusal caused the blockade or U.S. policy toward Qatar.
description_long: In June 2017, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Egypt severed diplomatic relations with Qatar and imposed a blockade. President Donald Trump publicly backed the coalition’s action. At the same time, the Kushner family was seeking foreign financing for 666 Fifth Avenue, its heavily indebted Manhattan property. The overlap drew conflict-of-interest scrutiny because the president’s family had business interests tied to foreign capital while he was taking a position in a regional dispute. The two developments are documented, but their timing does not show that a Qatari financing decision caused the blockade or Trump’s support for it. There is no established evidence that Jared Kushner’s property financing drove U.S. policy toward Qatar. The episode illustrates the appearance of competing public and private interests without proving a causal connection. Trump later softened his public stance as the administration pursued mediation. The blockade and the family’s financing search remain distinct events, and the available account supports scrutiny of their coincidence rather than a claim that one triggered the other.

title: Calls NATO 'Obsolete'
description_short: In an interview, Trump called NATO obsolete.
description_medium: In January 2017, President-elect Donald Trump called NATO “obsolete,” saying the alliance had not addressed terrorist attacks. Germany’s foreign minister said the remark had caused anxiety among alliance members and conflicted with defense secretary-designate James Mattis’s support for NATO. The comments came days before Trump’s inauguration.
description_long: In interviews published on January 15, 2017, President-elect Donald Trump called NATO “obsolete” and argued that it had failed to address terrorism. The remarks raised concerns among allied governments ahead of his inauguration. German Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said NATO foreign ministers viewed the comments with anxiety, and he noted that Trump’s position appeared to conflict with that of his incoming defense secretary, James Mattis, who had affirmed the alliance’s importance. NATO’s collective-defense commitment was central to European security, particularly amid tensions with Russia, so uncertainty about U.S. support mattered to allies. Trump also said the alliance needed to change how members shared the costs of defense. The interview did not announce a U.S. withdrawal or end NATO’s treaty obligations; it signaled a change in tone from the incoming president and prompted public reassurance from European officials. The episode set an early test for transatlantic relations: whether Trump’s campaign-era criticism would translate into a change in U.S. policy after he took office. The alliance continued, while the debate over burden-sharing remained active.

title: Grants Posthumous Pardon to Jack Johnson
description_short: Trump granted a posthumous pardon to boxer Jack Johnson.
description_medium: On May 24, 2018, President Donald Trump granted a posthumous pardon to boxer Jack Johnson, the first Black heavyweight boxing champion. Johnson had been convicted under the Mann Act in 1913. The case became a symbol of racially discriminatory prosecution, and the pardon addressed a conviction imposed more than a century earlier.
description_long: President Donald Trump granted a posthumous pardon to boxer Jack Johnson on May 24, 2018. Johnson, the first Black heavyweight champion, had been convicted under the Mann Act in 1913 after crossing state lines with Lucille Cameron, a white woman he later married. His prosecution came amid intense racial hostility toward Johnson, whose success and defiance of segregation provoked public backlash. The pardon followed years of advocacy by supporters who argued that the case had been racially motivated. Trump announced the pardon after speaking with Sylvester Stallone and other advocates. Johnson had died in 1946, so the pardon could not change his life or restore the years he spent in prison. It formally addressed a conviction widely viewed as unjust and brought renewed attention to how the Mann Act was used against Black men in the early twentieth century. The clemency was symbolic and historical, recognizing the injustice of the prosecution long after Johnson’s death.
